Bone Marrow Registry Gracey

By: Annalise Lubbe | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Time is running out for baby Gracey from Atlantis, a cancer patient waiting for a stem cell donor to give her a fighting chance. We went to meet her.

Unique Selling Point:
Gracey Green was diagnosed with juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia (JMML), a rare cancer of the blood that affects young children, and the only cure is to have a stem cell transplant from a matched donor. According to the South African Bone Marrow Registry (SABMR), people of colour are heavily underrepresented in the registry, making it difficult for patients with a diverse ethnic heritage to find a matching donor. For 14-month-old Gracelyn (Gracey) Green, this means that her chances for survival are slim without the help of community members and donors. But will a suitable donor be found in time to save the life of this child when she has already endured so much in such a short lifespan. She lost her mom at 6 months old, gone through three blocks of chemotherapy and at this stage there is little hope to find a donor that will be a suitable match.

Summary:
14-month-old Gracey Green lost her mom in a fire at the family’s home in Atlantis in June last year. It was a tragic event that claimed the lives of several family members. Gracey was put in the care of her loving aunt, Liezel Solomons, who was close to Gracey’s mom Shanique.

It was a tough time for Liezel who battled to come to terms with the death of her niece and now had to deal with a new baby when she had a family of her own to take care of. But Liezel knew it was the right thing to do.

Shortly after Liezel took on the role as mom, she noticed an unusual swelling in her belly and took Gracey to the local doctor who immediately referred her to the Red Cross Hospital for tests. The tests revealed Gracey had an enlarged spleen, liver and lymph nodes which doctors diagnosed as JMML where white blood cells don’t develop as they should. Since then Gracey had been on three blocks of chemotherapy to slow down the spread of the cancer cells. But her condition did not improve.

Gracey's only chance is to find a donor that will match her stem cells in order to stop the cancer from claiming her life. But with so few people of colour in South Africa on the donor registry, her chance is one in 100 000.

At present the future is uncertain but what is certain is the love of her aunt and the hope of the family that they will find a suitable donor in time to save Gracey’s life. Gracey’s father, Lorenzo, finds it difficult to bear the loss of his wife and can’t come to terms with the illness of his little baby on top of it all. For Liezel the cross was almost unbearable. Besides losing her niece she lost her father, her mother and her brother on that fateful night that Gracey’s mom suffocated from the smoke in the house. Now the hope of the family is pinned on finding a donor for little Gracey that she may live.


Further information:
The South African Bone Marrow Registry (SABMR) is facilitating a donor match for Gracey and hope that they will find a suitable stem cell match in time. In most cases family members, especially siblings are most suitable but then, only 30% of patients are lucky enough to find a suitable match among their relatives. Due to the SABMR’s Patient Assistance Programme.

Our story:
We will interview Gracey’s aunt, Liezel Solomon; the oncologist, Prof Alan Davidson; Dr Charlotte Ingram, Medical Director of the South African Bone Marrow Registry and a short interview with the father, Lorenzo. He is not in a good emotional space so it might be a very short comment we get from him. The aunt speaks well and is holding it all together. Dr. Ingram can talk about the shortage of donors and the Prof about the treatments Gracey received and hope for a donor match.

We will film at the Red Cross hospital on Thursday where the interviews with the medical team will take place. We will also film the aunt and baby Gracey at the hospital where a blood testing will be performed.

We will interview the aunt at her home in Atlantis with scenes of baby Gracey. We will also film the family home where the fire broke out and use photos to add to the story.

In summary, the story is one of tragedy but also one of hope that as long as you believe there is an outcome.

Script:


Script: Time is running out for baby Gracey
Duration: 5 minutes
Date: 4 March 2022

Up sound piano

V/O At fourteen months Gracelyn Green is learning about the world around her.

Up sound piano

V/O Gracey was only 6 months old when she lost her mother in a terrible accident.

Up sound music

V/O In June last year Gracey’s mother Shanique, and several other family members were trapped in a family home in Atlantis when a fire broke out. Gracey’s aunt Lizel, who lived nearby, arrived at the scene within minutes.

Lizel Solomons - Gracey’s aunt: So I ran into the house, one of the guys came out with Shanique. While I was sitting next to her I realised my mom was laying next to me and my brother was laying on the other side. So I spoke to Shanique, I begged her to breathe, I told her that Gracey needs her but it was like water running through your hands.

Link: Gracey was saved at the last moment when Shanique passed her 6-month-old baby through the window to her uncle.

V/O Gracey’s father Lorenzo, was devastated.

Lorenzo Erasmus – Gracey’s father: Ons het groot planne gehad (We had big plans.) Ons het saam besluit dat ons wil n babatjie he. (Together we decided to have a baby.) Sy beteken baie vir my. (She means a lot to me.)

Derek Watts: How close were you to Shanique?

Lizel Solomons: She used to call me Lala. One thing that she always believed was that Lala can fix anything. And the last day of her life, that was not the case. I couldn’t fix it, I couldn’t make it right.

Derek Watts: How have you coped?

Lizel Solomons: Hmm.

V/O Not only did Lizel lose her best friend that day - She lost parents and brother in the fire. But there was no time to grieve. Lizel could see Gracey needed a mom.

Up sound

Lizel Solomons: She was crying endlessly for hours. At one point I said to Lorenzo her dad I think we might have to take her to a doctor because something might be wrong.

V/O At first Lizel thought it was teething that was causing Gracey’s discomfort but then they saw her swollen tummy and took Gracey to the Red Cross War Memorial Children’s Hospital. Tests revealed a cancer of the blood - juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia. Professor Alan Davidson broke the news to the family.

Derek Watts: Prof, in layman's terms can you describe her condition?

Prof Alan Davidson - Head Paediatric Oncology: Red Cross War Memorial Children’s Hospital - So juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia or JMML for short. This is a chronic leukemia. It is characterised usually by a very large spleen in the tummy. And there bonemarrow which is filled up with these excess and useless white cells. So they need to have blood transfusions and blood products and they have a higher chance of getting infections.

Lizel Solomons: I couldn’t stop asking really, why, again us as a family, why?

Lorenzo Erasmus: Jy wonder nou hoekom gebeur alles nou met jou. (You wonder why everything is happening to you.) Daar is a klomp vrae. (There are a lot of questions you ask.)

Up sound - Gracey crying

Prof Alan Davidson: Unfortunately unlike the typical leukemia it doesn’t respond to the traditional chemotherapy regimens which we use for the other forms of leukemia.

V/O. After three sets of chemotherapy failed, Gracey’s only chance was to receive a stem cell transplant.

Prof Alan Davidson: The ideal donor is a matched sibdonor where you look for a ten out of ten match and a sibling who is fully matched is the best donor.

V/O But Gracey has no siblings so the search had to widen. For thirty years the South African Bone Marrow Registry has been matching patients with donors. Gracey’s case poses a challenge for them. Of the 76 000 donors on the registry only 7.8% are coloured.

Link: Finding a suitable match for baby Gracey is like finding a needle in a haystack, like winning the lotto because not many people of colour are registered on the database.

Dr Charlotte Ingram - Medical Director: South African Bone Marrow Registry.
We know that the chances of finding a match in that population for Gracey are probably the highest there and that is one of the reasons we are going back to her community is to be there and to see if we can’t find a match there.

V/O In a special drive for Gracey the South African Bone Marrow Registry went out to Atlantis, in full force, to find a suitable match.

Lizel Solomons: I was told that it would be one in 100 000 people that might be a match to Gracey. But we cannot sit and do nothing.

Derek: Lizel what are your hopes and prayers for Gracey?

Lizel Solomons: A long life. A long healthy life and it starts with what we are doing now. Finding a donor for her. And someone could be that gift of long life for her.

Up sound….Princess Gracey
